_doc.purpose: A FRAMEWORK, not a catalogue. Nine commodities, chosen to exercise every case in rome/data/world/COMMODITIES.md: something mined (iron, copper, coal, gold), something grown (wool), something manufactured from another commodity (cloth from wool/flax, copper wire from copper), and something obtainable only by trade (coffee, cotton). Read COMMODITIES.md before touching this file; it explains every field.

confidence_key.B: probable, scholarly consensus, contested in detail
confidence_key.C: author's estimate or inference, order of magnitude only

_doc.not_integrated: sim/engine/core.py's Sim class does not read this file. See COMMODITIES.md section 11 (hard problems) for the migration this would take.

iron.name: Iron

produced_by.note: generic capacity via Sim.open_mine('iron', t_per_yr); capex/opex in economy.py.MINE_CAPEX_PER_T_YR

iron.consumed_by_note: hundreds of nodes; iron_bar_kg alone appears in well over 100. Not enumerated here, see commodity_consumers() in commodities.py.
iron.notes: The bloomery-to-blast-furnace-to-coke progression changes the FUEL a tonne of iron costs (see resources.json constraints.iron_*), not the tonnes of iron itself, so it is not modelled here as an iron-output multiplier. A second pass that wants 'a blast furnace makes iron more available' should multiply national_output, the way gold's water pump does below, once a furnace-throughput figure is estimated.

copper.name: Copper

produced_by.note: generic capacity via Sim.open_mine('copper', t_per_yr); capex/opex in economy.py.MINE_CAPEX_PER_T_YR

copper.notes: This is the commodity the copper-wire demand-propagation demo depends on: see copper_wire.recipe below and COMMODITIES.md section 7.

copper_wire.name: Copper wire, drawn
copper_wire.output_source: derived: min(national_manufacturing_capacity_t_per_yr * best built multiplier, copper_available_t_per_yr / recipe ratio). No independent geological figure exists for a manufactured good.
copper_wire.manufacturing_capacity_note: Order-of-magnitude estimate for empire-wide smith-hours available for wire drawing before any dedicated bench exists: a handful of workshops, not an industry. This is the labour/plant ceiling that mfg_wire_drawing and drawplate_wire multiply; see COMMODITIES.md section 9 for why this is a flat multiplier and not an actual labour-market model.
copper_wire.market_share_note: Unlike a raw ore, a manufactured good bought from an ordinary smith is not restricted by imperial mining concessions, so the reachable share of national output is much higher than copper's own 0.03. [C] estimate.
copper_wire.recipe_note: A 5% mass loss drawing wire through a plate (scale, offcuts, re-melts). Order of magnitude, not measured.

produced_by.note: The drawplate itself: the founding technology for drawn (as opposed to hammered) wire.
A dedicated wire-drawing bench, water- or hand-powered; [C] estimate of throughput over an ad hoc drawplate.

copper_wire.notes: This is the commodity the brief's 'kilometres of copper wire' scenario is built on: see COMMODITIES.md section 7.1 for the worked failure, and el2_three_wire_distribution_system in the tech tree (5,000 kg of copper_wire_kg in one build) for the real node that would trigger it at scale.

coal.name: Coal

produced_by.note: generic capacity via Sim.open_mine('coal', t_per_yr). resources.json is explicit that the 5,000 t/yr baseline is a ceiling of WILL, not of geology: Rome does not coke coal, so almost nobody wants it yet.

coal.notes: coal_coke, the tech node that actually matters for iron output, changes what iron's fuel line item costs (see resources.json constraints.iron_blast_furnace_coke), not coal's own national output. Left as a note rather than a produced_by multiplier for the same reason iron's blast furnace is: this pass does not model furnace-level fuel substitution, only commodity-level supply and demand.

gold.name: Gold
gold.price_source: data/prices.json:gold_kg, from the aureus at 7.27g = 25 denarii
gold.price_ceiling_note: Gold's ceiling is lower than a base-metal's because it is already the thing prices are implicitly measured against; letting its OWN price run away is a unit problem, not a scarcity signal.
gold.monopoly_note: Not because gold itself is scarce information, but because a SPECIFIC rich vein worked with technology nobody else in the empire has (hydraulic mining, cyanide leaching) is, in practice, yours alone until the knowledge spreads.

produced_by.note: generic capacity via Sim.open_mine('gold', t_per_yr); capex/opex in economy.py.MINE_CAPEX_PER_T_YR (160,000 den per t/yr to sink, the highest in the table)

[C] estimate: mechanical dewatering lets a shaft go deeper and work ore a hand-bailed mine would flood out of. Order of magnitude, not measured; Roman hydraulic engineering at Las Medulas (ruina montium, sluicing) already demonstrates large-scale water-powered gold extraction, so this is a real lever, not an invented one.

[C] estimate. Cyanide leaching (historically, the 1890s Witwatersrand) is commonly credited with making previously uneconomic LOW-GRADE ore worth processing at all, effectively multiplying recoverable gold from a given tonnage of rock by a large factor; 7x is an order-of-magnitude figure for that jump, not a measured Roman one, since the process is a millennium and a half early.

gold.notes: met_mine_pumping and mt2_cyanidation together give roughly 21x baseline (3.0 * 7.0), which is where the brief's '20x the gold of the rest of the country combined' figure comes from: a single mine holding both technologies, sized comparably to a typical Roman working, plausibly outproduces the rest of the empire's ungraded, unpumped workings combined. See sim/demo_commodities.py for the worked arithmetic. This is illustrative, not a claim that Roman Spain could actually have supported a mine 20x its historical output; it is the exact kind of asymmetry this whole game is built to let one person create.

wool.name: Wool (raw, scoured)
wool.output_source: DERIVED, not sourced: 65,000,000 (data/civilizations/rome_100ad.json population) times an assumed 1.5 kg of raw wool consumed per person per year (a plausibility estimate for pre-industrial per-capita wool use, not a scholarly figure) gives 97,500 t/yr, rounded. This is the weakest number in this file and should be the first one a second pass replaces with an actual source.
wool.market_share_note: [C] estimate: wool, unlike a metal ore, is not under any concession system, so an ordinary buyer's reachable share is high.

produced_by.note: baseline pastoral wool production, already part of Rome's starting economy
[C] estimate: selective breeding for fleece raises yield per animal on the same pasture; real and directionally correct (compare later Merino selection), figure is illustrative.

wool.notes: wool is the upstream commodity for cloth's recipe. Its own supply is comfortably above what the loom lineage can weave even at power-loom throughput (see cloth.national_manufacturing_capacity_t_per_yr), so in THIS data file wool is never the bottleneck for cloth; a second pass that wants sheep-pasture to matter needs a lower wool baseline or a much faster loom.

cloth.name: Woven cloth (wool or flax base, not distinguished in this pass)
cloth.material_keys_note: Lumping wool cloth (cloth_kg) with flax/linen cloth (linen_kg) is a deliberate simplification, flagged in COMMODITIES.md section 9: a linen shortage should not be hidden by a wool surplus, and a second pass should split these into two commodities with two recipes (wool and flax respectively).
cloth.output_source: derived: min(national_manufacturing_capacity_t_per_yr * best built loom multiplier, wool_available_t_per_yr / recipe ratio)
cloth.manufacturing_capacity_note: [C] order-of-magnitude estimate for empire-wide hand-weaving throughput at the warp-weighted-loom baseline. This is deliberately BELOW the wool-supply ceiling (100,000 t wool / 1.15 ratio =~ 87,000 t of cloth) so that at low loom technology, WEAVING LABOUR, not wool, is the binding constraint -- which is the actual historical story (wool was rarely the bottleneck; spinning and weaving labour was) and is also why 'automated looms make cloth more available' is a true statement about looms and not about sheep.
cloth.recipe_note: 1.15 kg raw wool per kg finished cloth: carding, spinning and weaving losses. Order of magnitude.

produced_by.note: baseline: the standard attested Roman loom
[C]: the treadle frees both hands for the shuttle, a real and large productivity jump, figure is illustrative

[C]: order-of-magnitude figure for a power-loom operator minding several machines versus one hand-weaver, roughly where the historical Industrial Revolution progression from Cartwright's 1785 loom to mid-19th-century multi-loom minding landed; not pinned to a single citation, see COMMODITIES.md section 4.2

cloth.notes: This is the commodity the brief's loom-and-balloon example is built on. hot_air_balloon needs 400 kg of linen_kg; see COMMODITIES.md section 4.2 for the worked demonstration and sim/demo_commodities.py / sim/test_regressions.py for the code that proves it.

cotton.name: Cotton (raw fibre)
cotton.import_capacity_note: [C] estimate for what the existing India and Egypt trade routes could plausibly carry in raw cotton if a buyer wanted it, before any dedicated cotton-specific shipping is built. Order of magnitude, not a documented tonnage.
cotton.market_share_note: trade_only commodities are not throttled by a domestic concession share; the whole import_capacity_t_per_yr IS the market, and geography's reach multiplier (not market_share) is what actually limits a buyer.
cotton.notes: No domestic production route exists for cotton in this data file, on purpose: Rome in 100 AD does not grow cotton, it buys it, from India and Egypt (already reachable by the monsoon route, per geography.json). This is the 'something only obtainable by trade' example.

coffee.name: Coffee (roasted beans)
coffee.material_keys_note: coffee_kg does not exist in data/prices.json. It is not a Roman-era good; see the anachronism note below.
coffee.price_source: NOT in prices.json (no Roman price exists to anchor to). [C] placeholder, loosely scaled off pepper and other long-haul spice-trade goods in the same file, for the sole purpose of giving monopoly_price() something to multiply.
coffee.import_capacity_note: [C] illustrative figure only; see the anachronism note.
coffee.anachronism_note: DELIBERATELY ANACHRONISTIC. Coffea arabica cultivation and coffee drinking are not attested before roughly the 9th to 15th centuries CE (Ethiopia, then Yemen). A Roman of 100 AD has no coffee to discover, let alone monopolise. This entry exists ONLY to exercise monopoly_price() end to end, in a case where the brief specifically asked for one: 'you know where coffee grows and how to process it, so you hold a monopoly and sell it at a margin.' Do not wire this into the Rome 100 AD game state; see COMMODITIES.md section 5.
coffee.notes: The single-region located_materials entry (arabia_horn only) plus a cost_multiplier of 15 is what makes the monopoly premise mechanically true here: nobody without your specific knowledge of where and how has any way to compete for this commodity at all.
